title: TFT achieves higher cooperation than Always Defect in iterated PD
statement: In the iterated Prisoner's Dilemma, Tit-for-Tat achieves a cooperation rate exceeding 50% when paired against Always Defect, despite the Nash equilibrium predicting zero cooperation.
evidenceSummary: Classical result from Axelrod (1980) tournament. TFT begins with cooperation and mirrors; initial cooperation survives only one round but the pattern is informative.

title: Always Cooperate is exploited to minimum payoff against Always Defect in PD
statement: In Prisoner's Dilemma, Always Cooperate paired against Always Defect yields Player 1 the minimum possible payoff (0) in every round, while Player 2 achieves the maximum payoff (5) in every round.
evidenceSummary: Direct consequence of payoff matrix structure. AC never defects, so AD gets the temptation payoff every round.

title: Mutual TFT achieves near-optimal joint payoff in Prisoner's Dilemma
statement: When both players use Tit-for-Tat in the iterated Prisoner's Dilemma, the cooperation rate approaches 100% and total joint payoff approaches the Pareto-optimal outcome (3+3=6 per round).
evidenceSummary: TFT-vs-TFT cooperates forever after the first round, achieving joint payoff of 6 vs Nash prediction of 2.

title: Nash equilibrium prediction fails as a behavioral model for iterated PD
statement: In iterated Prisoner's Dilemma experiments, observed cooperation rates with conditional strategies (TFT, Grim Trigger) systematically exceed the Nash equilibrium prediction of 0% cooperation, demonstrating that Nash equilibrium is a poor behavioral predictor in repeated settings.
evidenceSummary: Documented across all conditional strategy matchups. The folk theorem establishes theoretical support for cooperation in infinite-horizon games.

title: Stag Hunt exhibits equilibrium selection problem: risk vs Pareto dominance
statement: In Stag Hunt, (Stag, Stag) Pareto-dominates (Hare, Hare) but strategies with any uncertainty converge to the risk-dominant (Hare, Hare) equilibrium, demonstrating the equilibrium selection problem between payoff-dominance and risk-dominance.
evidenceSummary: Stag-Stag yields (5,5) while Hare-Hare yields (3,3). However, the risk of unilateral stag hunting yields 0, making Hare the safer choice.

title: Random play fails to coordinate on either Nash equilibrium in Stag Hunt
statement: Random strategies in Stag Hunt achieve coordination (both Stag or both Hare) less than 50% of the time, yielding average payoffs below both Nash equilibria and demonstrating the cost of coordination failure.
evidenceSummary: With 50/50 random play, coordination probability is 0.25+0.25=0.5. Mixed outcomes (Stag-Hare, Hare-Stag) yield (0,3) or (3,0), dragging down averages.

title: Anti-coordination equilibria emerge in Chicken when players avoid symmetric outcomes
statement: In the Chicken Game, rational strategy pairs tend toward anti-coordination Nash equilibria (Swerve-Straight, Straight-Swerve) rather than mutual cooperation or mutual defection, with the latter producing the catastrophically low (0,0) payoff.
evidenceSummary: Nash equilibria in Chicken are (Swerve, Straight) and (Straight, Swerve), both anti-coordination. (Straight, Straight) gives (0,0), the worst joint outcome.

title: Nash mixed strategy prevents exploitation in zero-sum games
statement: In Matching Pennies and Rock-Paper-Scissors, the Nash mixed strategy (uniform random) achieves near-zero expected payoff deviation, while deterministic strategies are systematically exploited by adaptive or random opponents.
evidenceSummary: Any pure strategy in zero-sum games has a best response that defeats it with probability 1. Only the Nash mixed strategy is unexploitable.

title: Deterministic strategies are exploitable in zero-sum games
statement: In Matching Pennies, always playing Heads (Always Cooperate) against a Nash Mixed opponent yields a Player 1 expected payoff of approximately 0 — the same as Nash mixed — because the Nash mixed opponent cannot exploit predictability. However, against a strategic opponent tracking patterns, deterministic strategies yield negative expected payoffs.
evidenceSummary: Matching Pennies Nash mixed ignores opponent's action. Against non-adaptive opponents, any strategy yields 0. Exploitation requires tracking.

title: Pure coordination games trivially achieve optimal outcome with deterministic strategies
statement: In the Pure Coordination Game, strategy pairs where both players make the same deterministic choice (both Always Left or both Always Right) trivially achieve 100% Nash equilibrium rate and maximum joint payoff (4+4=8 per round), compared to 50% coordination rate with random play.
evidenceSummary: Any deterministic strategy that makes the same choice achieves perfect coordination. The challenge is misalignment between heterogeneous strategies.

title: Cooperation rate systematically exceeds Nash prediction in social dilemmas under repeated play
statement: Across Prisoner's Dilemma and Chicken Game experiments, strategies employing conditional cooperation (TFT, Grim Trigger, Generous TFT) achieve cooperation rates significantly above the Nash equilibrium prediction, supporting the folk theorem: repeated interaction sustains cooperation that one-shot analysis predicts should not exist.
evidenceSummary: The folk theorem (Aumann, Shapley, 1976) establishes that in infinitely repeated games, cooperation can be sustained as a Nash equilibrium through trigger strategies. Our experiments confirm this empirically.
